evidence: Etymonline: from Latin (ars) logica, from Greek (he) logike (techne) '(the) reasoning (art)', from logikos, from logos 'reason, idea, word'.

SEP: use of 'critical thinking' as an educational goal goes back to Dewey (1910), who defined reflective thinking as 'active, persistent and careful consideration of any belief or supposed form of knowledge in the light of the grounds that support it' (Dewey 1910: 6).
How We Think (Gutenberg text): 'The essence of critical thinking is suspended judgment; and the essence of this suspense is inquiry...'
forall x: 'we sometimes use the word argument to talk about belligerent shouting matches... They are not arguments, in our sense; they are just disagreements.'
Van Cleave 1.1: 'An argument is a set of statements, some of which (the premises) attempt to provide a reason for thinking that some other statement (the conclusion) is true.'
Van Cleave 1.2: ask whether there is a statement someone is trying to establish as true by basing it on some other statement; 'arguments always require at least two separate statements'.
Van Cleave 1.1 contrasts Sally 'simply asserting' her view in a heated exchange with her later 'offering a reason' for it, which is an argument.
APA blog: the 'Argument Clinic' sketch is from Monty Python's Flying Circus, episode 29, 'The Money Programme' (1972); the customer gets mere contradiction.

APA blog quotes: 'An argument is a connected series of statements to establish a definite proposition... It isn't just contradiction', and uses the sketch to introduce the philosophical conception of argument.
Van Cleave 1.1: a statement can be true or false; 'The Nile is a river in northeastern Africa' is one; 'The Yangtze is a river in Japan is still a statement; it is just a false statement'.
Van Cleave 1.1: 'Both premises and conclusions are statements'; non-statements are those where 'it doesn't make sense to ask whether those sentences are true or false'.
forall x: 'Are you sleepy yet?'... the question itself is neither true nor false; questions will not count as sentences, but answers will.
forall x: commands like 'Wake up!' are neither true nor false; 'Ouch!' is sometimes called an exclamatory sentence, but it is neither true nor false.
OpenStax College Success 7.4: 'Facts are verifiable'; 'mice are animals is a fact'. Van Cleave 1.9 calls descriptive statements claims about what is in fact the case.
OpenStax 7.4: you could find sources that validate or discredit the statement; even if incorrect, 'the statement itself is still a fact, just an erroneous one'.
OpenStax 7.4: 'opinions are beliefs without supporting evidence'; 'Blue is the best color' is an opinion; 'mice make the best pets is an opinion'.

Van Cleave 1.9: a normative statement is about what ought to be true 'relative to some standard of evaluation (for example, a moral or legal standard)'; indicated by 'should' and words such as good, bad and ought; descriptive statements say what is the case.
IEP Argument: 'The reasons offered within the argument are called premises, and the proposition that the premises are offered for is called the conclusion.'

Etymonline: premise from Medieval Latin praemissa '(the proposition) set before', from praemittere 'send forward, put before'; conclusion (etymonline.com/word/conclusion) from Latin concludere 'to shut up, enclose', from claudere 'to shut'.
Van Cleave 1.1: numbered premises with the conclusion last, denoted by 'therefore', is 'standard argument form'; forall x: 'The three dots on the third line of the argument are read therefore.'

forall x: 'a single sentence can contain a complete argument... The butler has an alibi; so they cannot have done it'; the conclusion can come at the beginning ('The gardener did it. After all, it was either the butler or the gardener. And the butler didn't do it.') or in the middle.
forall x: 'these words are often used to indicate an argument's conclusion: so, therefore, hence, thus, accordingly, consequently'.
Van Cleave 1.2, Table 1 premise indicators: since, because, for, as, given that (plus others); the IEP lists because, since, for and as.

IEP: 'these expressions do not always function in these ways, and so their mere use does not necessitate the presence of an argument.' Van Cleave 1.2 uses 'I have been running competitively since 1999' as a one-statement non-argument.
IEP: 'An enthymeme is an argument which is presented with at least one component that is suppressed.'
Van Cleave 1.9: an argument often won't explicitly state a premise needed for it to be valid; 'Making missing premises explicit is a central part of reconstructing arguments in standard form.'

Van Cleave 1.9: 'The principle of charity states that when reconstructing an argument, you should try to make that argument... as strong as possible'; for missing premises, supply the most plausible premises needed.
Van Cleave 1.9: an argument for a normative conclusion ('the state should...') depends 'on a normative premise which is not explicitly stated'.
Van Cleave 1.3: 'sometimes we already know that a statement or claim is true and we are trying to establish why it is true rather than that it is true... is an explanation.'

IEP: explaining 'is designed to increase the audience's comprehension', arguing 'is aimed at enhancing the acceptability of a standpoint'; the arguer believes the standpoint is not yet acceptable, the explainer that the explanandum is already accepted.
IEP: 'A: Why did this metal expand? B: It was heated and all metals expand when heated. B offers explanatory reasons for the explanandum.'

Van Cleave 1.4: 'very often arguments and explanations have a more complex structure'; IEP: 'An extended argument is an argument with at least one premise that a reasoner attempts to support explicitly.'

IEP extended-argument example: 'I just searched the kitchen and I did not find the keys. So the keys are not in the kitchen. The keys are either in the kitchen or the bedroom... So, the keys must be in the bedroom.'

Van Cleave 1.4: B 'acts as a premise for the main conclusion but is also itself the conclusion of further premises, we refer to B as an intermediate conclusion... one and the same statement can act as both a premise and a conclusion.'
Van Cleave 1.4: 'A subargument... is a part of an argument that provides indirect support for the main argument'; the main conclusion is supported without supporting a further claim.

How We Think (Gutenberg): cases 'taken, almost verbatim, from the class papers of students'; 'down town on 16th Street a clock caught my eye... the hands pointed to 12.20... an engagement at 124th Street, at one o'clock.'

How We Think: an hour down on a surface car, so 'twenty minutes late' returning that way; subway express 'quicker than the elevated' and 'nearer'; 'I concluded in favor of the subway, and reached my destination by one o'clock.'

IEP Validity and Soundness: the author of a deductive argument 'always intends that the premises provide the sort of justification for the conclusion whereby if the premises are true, the conclusion is guaranteed to be true as well.'

forall x: 'Either the butler or the gardener did it. The butler didn't do it. Therefore the gardener did it'; if the premises are true, only one option is left; 'the conclusion follows from the premises. We call arguments that have this property valid.'

forall x: a case in which the premises are true and the conclusion is not is 'a counterexample to the argument. If there is a counterexample to an argument, the conclusion cannot be a consequence of the premises.'

forall x: 'If the driver did it, the maid didn't do it. The maid didn't do it. Therefore the driver did it.' is not guaranteed: in the scenario where some third person did it, both premises are true and the conclusion false.
SEP Aristotle's Logic 3.1: 'Deductions are one of two species of argument recognized by Aristotle. The other species is induction (epagoge)... argument from the particular to the universal.'

IEP: valid 'if and only if it takes a form that makes it impossible for the premises to be true and the conclusion nevertheless to be false'; an argument can be valid even if a premise is actually false.

forall x: 'Oranges are either fruit or musical instruments. Oranges are not fruit. Therefore Oranges are musical instruments... If both premises are true, then the conclusion just has to be true. So the argument is valid.'
IEP: 'These arguments share the same form: All A are B; No B are C; Therefore, No A are C. All arguments with this form are valid.'
IEP: 'All toasters are items made of gold. All items made of gold are time-travel devices. Therefore, all toasters are time-travel devices.' The premises are not true, yet the argument is valid.
forall x: 'London is in England. Beijing is in China. Therefore Paris is in France. The premises and conclusion of this argument are, as a matter of fact, all true, but the argument is invalid.'
forall x 2.4, verbatim: 'It is often said that logic doesn't care about feelings. Actually, it doesn't care about facts, either.'
IEP: 'A deductive argument is sound if and only if it is both valid, and all of its premises are actually true'; a valid argument with true premises must have a true conclusion.

forall x: 'when you want to rebut an argument, you have two options: you can show that (one or more of) the premises are not true, or you can show that the argument is not valid. Logic, however, will only help you with the latter!'
Van Cleave 1.7: 'The relevant disciplines to consult if you want to know whether a particular statement is true is almost never logic!'
forall x: London/Beijing/Paris is invalid yet its conclusion is true; the oranges argument shows validity alone does not settle truth, so a flawed argument's conclusion can still be true.

SEP: 'Aristotle's logical works contain the earliest formal study of logic that we have'; 'Aristotle's most famous achievement as logician is his theory of inference, traditionally called the syllogistic.'

Knachel 3.6: three categorical propositions (two premises and a conclusion) featuring exactly three classes, each in exactly two propositions; SEP: the shared term is the middle term, and the conclusion joins the two not shared.
Linda Hall Library: 'John Venn, an English philosopher... In 1880, Venn introduced a new logical device that came to be known as a Venn diagram'; circles that intersect.
Knachel 3.6: draw three overlapping circles, depict the premises 'using shading and Xs', then ask whether the premises guarantee the conclusion, i.e. whether the picture shows it.
Knachel 3.6: 'In cases of indeterminacy, draw Xs straddling boundary lines'; when the X may or may not be in the needed region, the premises do not guarantee the conclusion, so the form is invalid.

Van Cleave 2.7: the proposition after 'if' is the antecedent and after 'then' the consequent; 'The conditional statement above is not asserting either of these atomic propositions... it is telling us about the relationship between them.'
Van Cleave 2.7: 'there is only one scenario in which we count the conditional false: when the antecedent is true and the consequent false', illustrated with raining and the ground not wet.
Van Cleave 2.11: 'modus ponens which is Latin for way that affirms': p implies q; p; therefore q; the form passes the truth table test, so 'any argument that has this same form is valid.'
Van Cleave 2.11: 'modus tollens, which is Latin for the way that denies': p implies q; not q; therefore not p; a valid form of inference.

IEP Fallacies, Affirming the Consequent: 'often mistaken for Modus Ponens'; example 'If she's Brazilian, then she speaks Portuguese. Hey, she does speak Portuguese. So, she is Brazilian.' Its form is an invalid form.

IEP: 'Noticing that she speaks Portuguese suggests that she might be Brazilian, but it is weak evidence by itself, and if the argument is assessed by deductive standards, then it is deductively invalid.'

IEP: denying the antecedent is to 'deny the antecedent of a conditional and then suppose that doing so is a sufficient reason for denying the consequent. This formal fallacy is often mistaken for Modus Tollens.'

Van Cleave 2.7: 'If you pass all the exams, you will pass the course'... 'When I assert E implies C I am not asserting anything about the situation in which E is false... that doesn't mean there aren't other ways of passing the course.'

IEP Deductive and Inductive Arguments: 'Inductive arguments, by contrast, are said to be strong or weak... A strong inductive argument is said to be one whose premises render the conclusion likely.'

Van Cleave 1.8: 'Tweets is a healthy, normally functioning bird... Tweets probably flies'; adding 'Tweets is 6 ft tall and can run 30 mph' means the conclusion would no longer be supported (an ostrich or emu).

SEP Abduction: abduction, often called Inference to the Best Explanation, concludes to what best explains the evidence; 'In these examples, the conclusions do not follow logically from the premises.'

SEP Abduction: in abductive examples 'the conclusions do not follow logically from the premises'; the Tim and Harry conclusion can be false though the premises are true.

Popular Science Monthly, August 1878 (Wikisource): 'Illustrations of the Logic of Science. Sixth paper: Deduction, Induction, and Hypothesis', which inverts one bean-bag syllogism into the three forms.

Peirce 1878: 'Suppose I enter a room and there find a number of bags, containing different kinds of beans. On the table there is a handful of white beans... one of the bags contains white beans only. I at once infer... that this handful was taken out of that bag.'

Peirce 1878: Deduction: Rule 'All the beans from this bag are white', Case 'These beans are from this bag', Result 'These beans are white'; induction infers the rule from case and result; hypothesis infers the case from rule and result.
Peirce 1878, verbatim: 'As a general rule, hypothesis is a weak kind of argument.' SEP Peirce: abductive inferences, 'which he also called hypotheses and retroductive inferences'.
IEP Fallacies, opening: 'A fallacy is a kind of error in reasoning... Fallacious reasoning should not be persuasive, but it too often is.'
SEP Fallacies: 'As an initial working definition of the subject matter, we may take a fallacy to be an argument that seems to be better than it really is.'

SEP Fallacies, abusive ad hominem: Thompson's wetlands proposal is rejected because of her arrest, yet 'although she broke the law, [she] may nevertheless have a very good plan'; a fallacious argument does not show its conclusion false (forall x likewise shows an invalid argument with a true conclusion).

IEP: 'The first known systematic study of fallacies was due to Aristotle in his De Sophisticis Elenchis (Sophistical Refutations)... He listed thirteen types of fallacies.' SEP: Aristotle discusses thirteen ways refutations can be sophistical.

Sophistical Refutations 1 (Pickard-Cambridge): 'some are really silver and others gold, while others... merely seem to be such... things made of litharge and tin seem to be of silver'; reasoning likewise, 'for inexperienced people obtain only, as it were, a distant view'.

Van Cleave 4.3: distinguish 'rhetorical techniques that are psychologically compelling' from 'rationally compelling arguments'; 'What makes something a fallacy is that it fails to be rationally compelling, once we have carefully considered it.'

IEP: ad hominem is to 'make an irrelevant attack on the person arguing and suggest that this attack undermines the argument itself. Ad Hominem means to the person.' Merriam-Webster: literally 'to the person'.

IEP: 'What she says about Johannes Kepler's astronomy of the 1600s must be just so much garbage. Do you realize she's only fifteen years old?' Her reasoning 'should stand or fall on the scientific evidence, not on the arguer's age'.

SEP: the abusive ad hominem says a view should not be accepted 'because they have some unfavorable property'; the circumstantial alleges the position is 'supported by self-interest rather than by good evidence'; the accused may still have a very good plan.

SEP 2.4: Locke 'is credited with intentionally creating a class of ad-arguments'; in the Essay (1690) he identified ad verecundiam, ad ignorantiam and ad hominem; 'Locke did not speak of ad-arguments as fallacies, that was left to others'. problem: The fact text is accurate, but card.logic.022.c5's headline 'John Locke named the ad hominem in 1690' overstates: Locke did not coin the Latin term (Galileo, among others, used the argument type earlier), and his ad hominem meant pressing someone with their own concessions, not the personal attack the level teaches. 'The name stuck, and so did the move' implies the same move.
proposed: In An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690), John Locke described ad hominem arguments, with other 'ad' arguments; he did not call them fallacies, which others did later. His ad hominem meant pressing people with their own principles or concessions; the personal-attack sense came later. (card.logic.022.c5: headline 'John Locke described the ad hominem in 1690. evidence: Van Cleave 4.3: 'Not every instance in which someone attacks a person's character is an ad hominem fallacy'; a defense lawyer may attack a witness's credibility; by contrast, once an argument is given 'we can assess the argument they have given on its own merits'.
IEP: 'The major difficulty with labeling a piece of reasoning an Ad Hominem Fallacy is deciding whether the personal attack is relevant or irrelevant.'

IEP Straw Man: 'attribute an easily refuted position to your opponent, one that the opponent would not endorse, and then proceed to attack the easily refuted position... believing you have thereby undermined... the opponent's actual position.'

Van Cleave 4.3: attacking position B, related to A 'but is much less plausible (and thus much easier to refute)... a straw man, a position that looks like the target position, but is actually not that position.'

IEP: the straw man is a position 'the opponent would not endorse', attacked in the belief that this undermines 'the opponent's actual position'; SEP: the straw man is a variant of ignoratio elenchi, where refuting a different claim leaves the real one untouched.
IEP: 'If the unfair and inaccurate representation is on purpose, then the Straw Man Fallacy is caused by lying'; in its example 'The Opponent is likely to respond with Wait! That's not what I said.'
IEP Smear Tactic: 'Smearing the opponent causes an Ad Hominem Fallacy. Smearing the opponent's argument causes a Straw Man Fallacy.'

IEP: a False Dilemma unfairly presents too few choices and implies a choice must be made among this short menu; Black-or-White 'limits you unfairly to only two choices'; False Dichotomy is listed as a name for it.
IEP: 'The fallacies of illegitimate presumption include Begging the Question, False Dilemma, No True Scotsman...'; the flaw is the limited menu of choices presented as the only ones.

IEP: 'A pollster asks you... is drunk on the job about (a) once a week, (b) twice a week, or (c) more times per week?... What about the choice of no times per week?' Think of the unpleasant choices as being the horns of a bull.
IEP: 'Will you contribute $20 to our environmental fund...'; 'everything is either black or not black, but not everything is either black or white.'

IEP Slippery Slope: a first step 'will probably lead to a second step that in turn will probably lead to another step... until a final step ends in trouble. If the likelihood of the trouble occurring is exaggerated, the Slippery Slope Fallacy is present.'

IEP: the slippery slope form 'occurs in both good arguments and faulty arguments. The quality of an argument of this form depends crucially on the strength of the probabilities in going from one step to the next.'
Van Cleave 4.2: 'Even if we grant that each link in the chain is individually probable, it doesn't follow that the whole chain... is probable.'
IEP: 'if the chain of reasoning A, B, C, D, ..., Z is about causes, then the fallacy is called the Domino Fallacy.'

IEP: circular reasoning 'occurs when the reasoner begins with what he or she is trying to end up with'; in begging the question premises presuppose the conclusion, 'there is no progress, and the arguer is essentially arguing by repeating the point.'

IEP: 'a dictionary contains a large circle of definitions... Because the dictionary is so informative, it is not considered as a whole to be fallacious. However, a small circle of definitions is considered to be fallacious.'
IEP, Begging the Question: 'The premise would here be termed reasonable if the arguer could defend it independently of accepting the conclusion that is at issue.'

Merriam-Webster: 'Beg the question is a phrase from formal logic; it's a 16th century translator's rendering of Aristotle's petitio principii. A better translation would have been assume the conclusion.'

Merriam-Webster: begging the question means 'to elicit a specific question as a reaction or response'; the formal-logic sense is 'lesser used'; it cites the raise-the-question use from Time and the Chicago Tribune as standard usage.

IEP: a red herring 'is also a digression that leads the reasoner off the track of considering only relevant information... An intentional false lead in a criminal investigation is another example of a red herring.'

Merriam-Webster: salting and slow smoking makes a herring 'turn red or dark brown, and gives them a very strong smell', a diversion for hunting dogs; etymonline: 'supposedly used by fugitives to put bloodhounds off their scent'.

SEP: 'The claim that Calgary is the fastest growing city in Canada, for example, is not defeated by a sound argument showing that it is not the biggest city in Canada' (ignoratio elenchi, or irrelevant conclusion).

IEP Tu Quoque: pointing out that the arguer doesn't practice what he or she preaches and supposing there must be an error in the preaching for only this reason; 'This is a kind of Ad Hominem Circumstantial Fallacy.' Merriam-Webster: Latin 'you too'.

SEP: 'if our neighbor advises us to exercise regularly and we reject her advice on the basis that she does not exercise regularly, we commit the tu quoque fallacy: the value of advice is not wholly dependent on the integrity of the advisor.'
IEP: 'Discovering that a speaker is a hypocrite is a reason to be suspicious of the speaker's reasoning, but it is not a sufficient reason to discount it.'
Merriam-Webster: 'A typical tu quoque involves charging your accuser with whatever it is you've just been accused of rather than refuting the truth of the accusation, an evasive strategy.'
IEP: 'When you defend your wrong action as being right because someone previously has acted wrongly, you are using the fallacy called Two Wrongs do not Make a Right.'

IEP Appeal to the People: suggesting 'too strongly' that a claim is correct because most everyone believes it; what most believe is somewhat likely true, but 'the fallacy occurs when this degree of support is overestimated.'

IEP: 'You should turn to channel 6. It's the most watched channel this year'; fallacious because it accepts 'the questionable premise that the most watched channel this year is, for that reason alone, the best channel for you.'

evidence: IEP Bandwagon: a claim is treated as correct 'simply because it's what most everyone is coming to believe'; 'The key ingredient that is missing from a bandwagon fallacy is knowledge that an item is popular because of its high quality.'

IEP: 'what most everyone believes is, for that reason, somewhat likely to be true... the fallacy occurs when this degree of support is overestimated'; to be distinguished from 'pointing out that many people have studied the claim and have come to a reasoned conclusion'.

IEP: 'Fallacies of relevance include fallacies that occur due to reliance on an irrelevant reason... Ad Hominem'; 'The fallacies of illegitimate presumption include Begging the Question, False Dilemma, No True Scotsman...'
IEP: 'Researchers in the field of fallacies disagree about... which is the best taxonomy of the fallacies.'
SEP: 'In the main, these fallacies spring from two fountainheads: Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations and John Locke's An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690).'

SEP Evidence: 'If E is evidence for some hypothesis H, then E makes it more likely that H is true... if E is evidence against H, then E makes it less likely'; 'smoke counts as evidence of fire, but not of impending rain', because it is a reliable indicator.

SEP Ethics of Belief 2.1: prudential norms aim 'at a kind of prudential or pragmatic value, and not at the truth per se'; it may be prudent, given your ends, to believe or withhold belief regardless of moderate evidence.

Clifford, The Ethics of Belief (1877), Wikisource: an emigrant-ship owner knew she was old and 'often had needed repairs'; refitting would 'put him to great expense'; he overcame his doubts, sincerely believed her safe, and 'she went down in mid-ocean'. SEP: repairs 'would be costly and cause significant delay'.

Clifford: suppose 'she made her voyage safely... Will that diminish the guilt of her owner? Not one jot.' He 'had acquired his belief not by honestly earning it in patient investigation, but by stifling his doubts'; 'he had no right to believe on such evidence'.
Clifford (Wikisource, Lectures and Essays text), verbatim: 'it is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.'

IEP Misplaced Burden of Proof: 'Committing the error of trying to get someone else to prove you are wrong, when it is your responsibility to prove you are correct. Person A: I saw a green alien from outer space... You can't prove I didn't.'
LII Wex: 'in criminal cases, the burden of proving the defendant's guilt is on the prosecution, and they must establish that fact beyond a reasonable doubt.'

LII Wex: a defendant 'is assumed to be innocent until they have been proven guilty'; the prosecutor 'is required to prove beyond a reasonable doubt' every element to convict, so an unproved case ends without conviction.
The Latin Library, Digest 22.3.2: 'Paulus 69 ad ed. Ei incumbit probatio qui dicit, non qui negat.'

IEP: 'A charge of fallacious reasoning always needs to be justified. The burden of proof is on your shoulders when you claim that someone's reasoning is fallacious... it is your responsibility to be able to give them if challenged.'

IEP: 'The Fallacy of Appeal to Ignorance comes in two forms: (1) Not knowing that a certain statement is true is taken to be a proof that it is false. (2) Not knowing that a statement is false is taken to be a proof that it is true.'

SEP 2.4: in An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690) Locke 'identified three kinds of arguments, the ad verecundiam, ad ignorantiam, and ad hominem'; Locke's text (Book IV, xvii) says 'this I call argumentum ad ignorantiam'.
IEP: 'It would be proper reasoning only if the proof attempts were quite thorough, and it were the case that, if the being or object were to exist, then there would be a discoverable proof of this.'

IEP Anecdotal Evidence: 'If you discount evidence arrived at by systematic search or by testing in favor of a few firsthand stories, then your reasoning contains the fallacy of overemphasizing anecdotal evidence.'
